source.title: New open problems related to old conjectures by Helleseth

accepted.question_text: For a map, or specifically a permutation, over a finite field, determine necessary and sufficient conditions under which multiplying the map by every nonzero field element preserves its Fourier spectrum; that is, characterize exactly when the spectrum of each scalar multiple is equal to the spectrum of the original map.

accepted.question_text: For any prime p, prove or disprove Helleseth's Three-Valued Conjecture: if a finite field has degree over its prime field equal to a power of two, then no invertible exponent over that field has a three-valued Fourier spectrum. The paper notes that the conjecture remains open for primes p greater than 3.

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1.5 (Helleseth Three-Valued Conjecture, 1976). For any prime , if is a power of two, then the spectrum of an invertible exponent is not three-valued. This conjecture remains open for .

accepted.question_text: Find an analogue of Katz's 2012 theorem for four-valued power-permutation spectra. Katz's theorem says that if a power permutation is three-valued, then it is singular, its exponent satisfies the relevant congruence condition, and its spectrum lies in the integers; the open problem asks for the corresponding structural theorem, if any, when the spectrum has four values.

Find an analogue of Theorem 3.5 for four-valued exponents.

accepted.question_text: Determine whether every nice exponent over prime fields of the characteristics tested in the authors' numerical experiment is necessarily one of the paradigmatic examples described in Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Here a nice exponent is an invertible exponent over a finite field for which the number of solutions of the associated differential equation takes at most a fixed small number of values as the right-hand side varies.

evidence.quote: Definition 6.1. Let be an invertible exponent over the finite field . We say that is a nice exponent over  if the number of solutions in of takes at most values as runs through . Remark 6.2. A -uniform exponent is nice.

As one can see in this example, the nice exponents are rare, and all have differential multiplicity . Surprisingly, this seems to be a general fact. Indeed, for the characteristics to , all the observed nice exponents have as a differential multiplicity. Problem 6.7. All nice exponents over the prime fields of characteristic were found in the numerical experiment [15], and they all correspond to the paradigmatic examples of Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Is this a general property?

accepted.question_text: For a finite field of odd characteristic, prove or disprove the nice-exponent conjecture: if an exponent over the field is nice, meaning its associated differential multiplicities take at most the specified small number of values, then 2 occurs as one of those differential multiplicities.

evidence.quote: We propose some conjectures based on our numerical evidence. Conjecture 6.8 (nice exponent). Let be an exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic. If is nice, then is a differential multiplicity.

accepted.question_text: For a finite field of odd characteristic, prove or disprove the stronger optimist conjecture: if an exponent over the field is invertible, then 2 occurs as a differential multiplicity for that exponent.

evidence.quote: We can make an even stronger conjecture. Conjecture 6.9 (optimist). Let be an exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic. If is invertible, then is a differential multiplicity.
